distractor_explanations.It makes the factories seem friendly: Sentinels are watchful guards, and the verb "dominated" pushes the tone toward imposing, not welcoming. This choice mistakes any comparison for a positive one—the simile's connotations are austere and oppressive.
distractor_explanations.It describes the color blue: The color word in the sentence is "gray," and no blue appears at all. More importantly, the simile's effect is about the character the smokestacks take on (guarding, looming), not about hue.
distractor_explanations.It compares factories to soldiers litera: The word "like" is the signal of a simile, which is figurative by definition—"literally" contradicts how similes work. Also, sentinels are guards standing watch, not soldiers in battle.

distractor_explanations.A clause cannot stand alone: This is backwards and incomplete. Independent clauses CAN stand alone; only subordinate clauses cannot. The defining difference between clauses and phrases is the subject–verb core, not stand-alone status.
distractor_explanations.A phrase is longer than a clause: Length has nothing to do with the distinction. A long phrase ("in the garden behind the old fence") can be longer than a short clause ("she ran").
distractor_explanations.They are the same thing: They are grammatically different: every clause contains a subject and verb; a phrase lacks one. Treating them as identical erases the distinction tested throughout the exam.

distractor_explanations.But: "But" is a coordinating conjunction (the FANBOYS set: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so), which joins equal elements, not a subordinate one.
distractor_explanations.Or: "Or" is also coordinating—it joins words, phrases, or clauses of equal grammatical rank.
distractor_explanations.And: "And" is the most common coordinating conjunction, not subordinating. A quick FANBOYS check eliminates all three distractors here.

distractor_explanations.Read faster: Speed reduces the processing time available for comprehension. Faster reading typically worsens recall—the misconception here is equating fluency with understanding.
distractor_explanations.Read silently without stopping: Removing pauses removes the metacognitive checkpoints (summarizing, questioning, connecting) that convert reading into memory. Silent endurance is not comprehension.
distractor_explanations.Skip difficult parts: The skipped parts become exactly the gaps in recall. Avoidance leaves the misconception untouched and compounds confusion later.

distractor_explanations.It is not important: Literary analysis rests on the premise that interpretation is informed by context—historical, cultural, biographical. Claiming it is unimportant contradicts the discipline.
distractor_explanations.Context only matters for old books: Contemporary texts carry political, cultural, and personal context too; today's novel is tomorrow's historical document. Age does not gate context.
distractor_explanations.Texts are self-contained: A purely formalist claim. While close reading matters, standardized analysis expects students to connect texts to the circumstances that shaped them.

distractor_explanations.Exaggeration: Exaggeration is hyperbole ("I've told you a million times"), not the pairing of contradictory terms.
distractor_explanations.Comparison with like/as: That is a simile. An oxymoron works by contradiction inside a single phrase, not by explicit comparison.
distractor_explanations.Repetition: Repetition (or alliteration for sounds) is a different device entirely; an oxymoron is defined by internal contradiction—"bittersweet," "deafening silence."

distractor_explanations.A grammatical error: A hook is a deliberate craft move, not an error. This distractor confuses style with mistake.
distractor_explanations.A conclusion: A hook sits at the opening of an essay; the conclusion is the opposite end. Position alone makes this wrong.
distractor_explanations.A bibliography entry: Bibliography entries belong to documentation at the end of a paper and serve attribution, not reader engagement.

distractor_explanations.Tell them they are wrong: A flat correction does not touch the underlying mental model ("longer decimal = bigger"), so the misconception survives the next problem. Effective feedback targets the model, not the answer.
distractor_explanations.Have them convert to fractions without e: This swaps one procedure for another without a conceptual anchor; comparing 1/50 and 1/2 still requires a model of magnitude to interpret.
distractor_explanations.Ask them to count the digits: This reinforces the very misconception—more digits is exactly why the student thinks 0.12 is larger. Practice built on a faulty rule entrenches it.

distractor_explanations.36: 36 is divisible by 9: the digit sum 3 + 6 = 9, and 36 = 4 × 9.
distractor_explanations.27: 27 = 3 × 9; digit sum 2 + 7 = 9. Only 28 fails the digit-sum test (2 + 8 = 10).

distractor_explanations.1 is too small: Size is irrelevant to primality, which is a structural property (the number of distinct factors), not a magnitude threshold.
distractor_explanations.1 is even: 1 is odd. And evenness is irrelevant anyway—2 is even and is the only even prime.
distractor_explanations.It is divisible by 1: Every integer is divisible by 1. A prime must have exactly two distinct positive factors; 1 has only one (itself), which is why it is excluded.

distractor_explanations.Confirm that 3(x + 2) is correct: It is not: 3(x + 2) expands to 3x + 6, which reads "three times the sum of a number and two." Confirming it cements the translation error.
distractor_explanations.Replace x with 3 and keep the expression: Substitution does not repair structure. The error is in how words were translated into operations, not in the value x takes.
distractor_explanations.Tell the student to reverse every operat: A blanket reversal rule misfires on most phrasings ("three more than" does not mean subtract 3). Better feedback unpacks the phrase piece by piece, as the correct choice does.

distractor_explanations.5: 5 appears twice, less often than 9 (three times). The mode is the most frequent value, not any repeated value.
distractor_explanations.3: 3 appears once. A value occurring once can never be the mode of this set.
distractor_explanations.11: 11 appears once and is the largest number—this distractor targets the common confusion between mode (most frequent) and maximum (largest).

distractor_explanations.Conic: Conic projections distort area away from their standard parallels; they are chosen for shape and mid-latitude maps, not area fidelity.
distractor_explanations.Mercator: Mercator is the classic cautionary example: it inflates area dramatically near the poles (Greenland looks the size of Africa). It preserves angles, not area.
distractor_explanations.Cylindrical: "Cylindrical" is a family of projections (Mercator is one), and they generally distort area, increasingly toward the poles.

distractor_explanations.Volcanic eruptions: Eruptions are climate and geology events with no causal role in plague transmission. This distractor swaps an environmental disaster for a disease vector.
distractor_explanations.War only: While wars moved people, the pandemic's geography tracks trade networks, not battle lines. "Only" also makes it false even as a partial cause.
distractor_explanations.Alien visitation: Not a historical cause at all. A throwaway distractor like this does not separate students with partial knowledge from students with none.

distractor_explanations.Four: Sometimes students count administrative agencies as a "fourth branch," but the Constitution establishes three. This distractor catches over-generalization from civics trivia.
distractor_explanations.Two: Missing the judicial branch is the most common version of this error—the courts are less visible in daily news than Congress or the President.
distractor_explanations.Five: No constitutional basis; likely a guess distractor with no specific misconception behind it.

distractor_explanations.A boundary between countries: The International Date Line is a calendar convention, not a political border, and it zigzags around territories precisely to avoid splitting them.
distractor_explanations.The equator: The equator is 0° latitude, dividing Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Latitude has nothing to do with the date change.
distractor_explanations.The Prime Meridian: The Prime Meridian is 0° longitude at Greenwich—the reference for time zones and longitude measurement, not where the date jumps by a day.

distractor_explanations.Population increase only: Rapid growth is one phase of the transition (when death rates fall before birth rates), not the model as a whole.
distractor_explanations.Population decrease: Decline is possible in the final stage, but the transition model describes the shift in rates, not any single direction of change.
distractor_explanations.Migration patterns: The demographic transition concerns birth and death rates over development, not migration. This distractor borrows a demographic word to mislead.

distractor_explanations.High birth and death rates: That is Stage 1, the pre-industrial baseline the model starts from.
distractor_explanations.Rapid population growth: That characterizes Stages 2–3, when death rates fall first and the gap between birth and death rates widens.
distractor_explanations.No population change: Too absolute. The final stage allows stability or decline; several developed countries are in Stage 5 with falling populations. "No change" erases that.

distractor_explanations.Ignoring the process: Not instruction at all—this distractor checks whether students can eliminate a non-answer before evaluating pedagogy.
distractor_explanations.Reading text: Reading about the amendment process is passive exposure. Students never rehearse the propose–debate–vote structure that the question asks them to internalize.
distractor_explanations.Memorizing amendments: Memorizing the amendments teaches the products of the process, not the process itself. The stem asks specifically about process understanding.

distractor_explanations.Digestion: Digestion breaks food down—what consumers do after eating. Plants do not ingest; they synthesize their own food.
distractor_explanations.Fermentation: Fermentation is an anaerobic breakdown process that releases small amounts of energy; it does not build glucose from light.
distractor_explanations.Respiration: Respiration is the reverse transaction: it consumes glucose to release energy, rather than producing glucose.

distractor_explanations.Nuclear energy converted to sound: No nuclear processes are involved in a rolling ball; this distractor pairs a real energy form with an irrelevant context.
distractor_explanations.Chemical energy converted to potential e: There is no fuel or food releasing chemical energy, and the ball loses height rather than gaining it.
distractor_explanations.Potential energy converted to kinetic en: That accounts for rolling downhill, but the stem's key event is slowing to a stop. "Only" makes it wrong—the kinetic energy also leaves as heat through friction.

distractor_explanations.Convergent: Convergent boundaries destroy or deform crust—subduction recycles it, collisions uplift it. They do not create new ocean floor.
distractor_explanations.Strike-slip: Strike-slip boundaries slide horizontally; crust is neither created nor destroyed, merely sheared.
distractor_explanations.Transform: Transform is the same category as strike-slip (the San Andreas Fault is the textbook example). New crust forms only where plates pull apart.

distractor_explanations.300 km/s: Off by a factor of 1,000. Nothing in everyday physics operates at this speed for light.
distractor_explanations.30,000 km/s: Off by a factor of 10—plausible-looking precisely because it has the right digits in the wrong magnitude.
distractor_explanations.3,000 km/s: Off by a factor of 100. The exam expects the approximation 300,000 km/s (about 186,000 miles per second).

distractor_explanations.Tell them they are wrong: Assertion without evidence leaves the misconception intact. Fossil sequences ARE the evidence; showing them teaches the correction.
distractor_explanations.Agree with them: Affirms a false belief—the deepest kind of harm a science teacher can do, because it must later be unlearned.
distractor_explanations.Skip fossils: Avoidance manages the lesson, not the learning. The misconception walks out of the classroom untouched.

distractor_explanations.Protein synthesis: Ribosomes carry out protein synthesis; the nucleus holds the instructions (DNA) but does not assemble proteins itself.
distractor_explanations.Cell movement: Movement comes from the cytoskeleton, cilia, or flagella—structures outside the nucleus.
distractor_explanations.Energy production: That is the mitochondrion's job (cellular respiration). The nucleus directs activity but does not power it.

distractor_explanations.Agree with them: Energy is conserved; agreeing institutionalizes a misconception that will resurface in thermodynamics and fail the student there.
distractor_explanations.Tell them it's wrong: Like most bare corrections, this does not replace the faulty model ("energy gets used up") with the conservation picture.
distractor_explanations.Skip the topic: The misconception is among the most persistent in physical science education. Skipping it guarantees it survives another year.

distractor_explanations.Neither exists: Both are foundational genetics terms with clear, observable referents—this distractor is a discard option with no misconception to diagnose.
distractor_explanations.They are the same: They are related but distinct: one is the inherited code, the other is its expression. Collapsing them erases the gene–trait link the exam tests.
distractor_explanations.Phenotype is genes; genotype is appearan: Exactly backwards—a swap error worth flagging because students who pick this have the right concepts attached to the wrong labels.

distractor_explanations.All cells are identical: Directly contradicts observable biology: a neuron, a muscle cell, and a blood cell share DNA but differ in structure and job.
distractor_explanations.Random chance: Differentiation is tightly regulated gene expression during development, not a lottery.
distractor_explanations.Specialization is inefficient: It is the opposite—division of labor among specialized cells is what makes complex multicellular life possible.

distractor_explanations.Magnetic attraction: An entirely different force. This distractor checks whether students can tell contact forces and field forces apart.
distractor_explanations.A force that aids motion: Friction's defining action is opposing relative motion. (It can enable grip or walking, but that is opposition applied usefully, not "aiding motion" as stated.)
distractor_explanations.Gravity on slopes: On a slope, that is the component of gravity parallel to the surface—a different force with a different cause.

distractor_explanations.Magnetic fields: Earth's magnetic field acts on compasses and charged particles, not on moving air masses; the Coriolis effect needs no magnetism.
distractor_explanations.It is a coincidence: The deflection is systematic—every moving object in the Northern Hemisphere veers right relative to the surface. A consistent pattern is the opposite of coincidence.
distractor_explanations.Gravity pulls sideways: Gravity acts toward Earth's center. The Coriolis deflection is horizontal and is an apparent force arising from observing motion on a rotating surface.
